opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underappreciated parts of the whole enterprise. We tend to tell the story of AI as a story about algorithms and compute, and those matter enormously, but if you look at where the real leaps have come from, there's almost always a dataset underneath that somebody went to great pains to create. ImageNet is the classic example. Before people could teach machines to see, someone had to sit down and decide that labeling millions of images was a worthwhile thing to do, and at the time it wasn't obvious that it was.

For me, working on olfaction, this is very concrete. Vision has cameras, audio has microphones, so for those senses the data already existed in digital form, just waiting to be learned from. Smell has nothing like that. There's no standard sensor that turns an odor into a file. So if you want a machine to understand smell, you can't just scrape the internet. You have to go out into the world and build the dataset yourself, molecule by molecule. That means working with trained human panelists who can describe what they smell in a consistent vocabulary, running careful experiments, and dealing with all the messiness of biology and human perception.

What I've come to believe is that this kind of data collection isn't grunt work you do before the interesting part starts. It's a scientific act in its own right. Deciding what to measure, how to measure it, and how to make those measurements reliable is where a lot of the insight lives. When we built a model that could predict what a molecule smells like from its structure, the modeling was important, but the thing that made it possible was having high-quality data that hadn't existed before.

And I think there's a broader lesson there. Many of the domains where AI could do the most good, in biology, chemistry, materials, and medicine, look more like smell than like images. The data isn't sitting around. So the next frontier isn't only better models; it's building the instruments, the experimental pipelines, and the communities that generate new kinds of data. If you can open up a new data modality, you open up a whole new territory for machine learning to explore, and that's tremendously exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response says some domains, including biology, lack readily available data and require researchers to create it, but it does not contrast biology’s research expectations with AI/ML’s expectation of obtaining data externally.

r002.rationale: It says that when data is unavailable, researchers may need to build it themselves: for smell, they “can't just scrape the internet” and “have to go out into the world and build the dataset yourself.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the thing that strikes me when you look at the big successes in machine learning is that almost none of them started with a clever algorithm. They started with data that already existed. Text was on the internet. Images were on the internet. Audio was on the internet. We had the raw material of human sight and hearing and language just lying around, and the models came along and learned from it.

Smell is the opposite case. There was no internet of smell. Nobody had been uploading the molecular composition of what they smelled every morning. So when we set out to build a model that could predict what a molecule smells like, we had to go and build the dataset more or less from scratch. And that changes the way you think about the whole problem, because the data collection stops being a preprocessing step and becomes the research.

A few things I've learned from that. The first is that you have to really respect the measurement. In olfaction, the sensor is a human being, and humans are noisy. People disagree about what things smell like, they get tired, they get habituated after the fifth sample. So a lot of the work is designing the protocol so that the noise averages out and the signal survives. You end up thinking like an experimental psychologist as much as a machine learning person.

The second is that the data you collect encodes your hypotheses about the problem, whether you want it to or not. Which molecules you pick, which descriptors you ask people to rate, how many panelists, all of that is a bet on what matters. And if you get the bet wrong, the model will happily learn the wrong thing with high confidence. So I've become a little suspicious of the idea that you can just collect a lot of data and the structure will emerge. It emerges from the choices you made.

And then the third thing, which I think is the exciting part, is that once you have a model, even an imperfect one, it starts telling you where to collect next. It tells you where it's uncertain, which regions of chemical space look weird, which predictions you should actually go smell. So you get this loop where the model is a participant in the data collection, and that loop is, to me, the actual engine. The dataset isn't a static thing you finish. It's something you grow in conversation with the model.

I'd generalize that beyond smell. I think the next big expansions of what AI can do are going to come in domains where the data doesn't exist yet, and the groups who figure out how to generate it carefully, physically, in the real world, are going to have a huge advantage. It's less glamorous than architecture work. But it's where the ceiling actually gets raised.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts domains where data already existed online with smell, where researchers had to build a dataset from scratch. It does not state a contrast between biology’s and AI/ML’s expectations about generating versus obtaining data.

r002.rationale: The candidate says expanding AI may depend on generating data carefully in domains where data does not yet exist, but does not mention vendors or their inability to supply it.

astra-6.text:
I think collecting new data is one of the most important ways to expand what AI can do. We spend a lot of time talking about models, but a model can only learn about the parts of the world that show up in its data. If something hasn’t been measured or digitized, it’s largely invisible to it.

Smell is a great example. We have enormous amounts of text and images, but we don’t have anything comparable for what molecules smell like. So the work starts with figuring out what to measure, how to measure it consistently, and how to connect those measurements to human perception.

That’s a scientific challenge as much as a machine learning challenge. And it creates this interesting loop: you collect data, train a model, look at where it struggles, and use that to decide what to measure next. You’re building the dataset and your understanding of the problem together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI models’ reliance on data, but does not contrast biology’s expectation of generating data with AI/ML’s expectation that data can be obtained externally.

r002.rationale: It describes collecting and measuring data, but does not state that researchers may need to collect it themselves because vendors cannot supply it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think collecting new data is one of the most powerful ways to expand what AI can do. We tend to focus on models and algorithms, but those models can only learn from the parts of the world we’ve figured out how to measure. If something isn’t represented in the data, making the model bigger doesn’t necessarily get you there.

Smell is a great example. We have these enormous datasets for images and language, but we don’t have the same kind of infrastructure for describing how molecules smell. So part of the scientific work is figuring out what to measure, how to collect reliable judgments, and how to connect those judgments to molecular structure.

That makes data collection much more than a preliminary step. You’re deciding which questions become possible to ask. And then you can build a loop: train a model, see where it’s uncertain or wrong, and go collect the measurements that would teach you the most.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes the value of collecting data but does not contrast biology’s expectation that researchers generate data with AI/ML’s expectation that data can be obtained externally.

r002.rationale: It says researchers may need to collect measurements when data is missing, but does not state that this is needed when vendors cannot supply them.
